title: The Shift to Agentic AI: Evidence from Codex
author: Drew Johnston · David Holtz · Alex Martin Richmond · Christopher Ong · Prasanna Tambe · Aaron Chatterji

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Assisted inequality: Productivity gains need not improve careers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s separation of technical capability from realized organizational and labour-market outcomes, then materially extends it by analysing delegated agentic workflows and identifying access, skills, workflow design, review and verification as complements required to capture value. Its cited evidence that automation-prone and collaborative jobs experience different demand and skill effects further supports the claim that productivity or adoption alone does not determine career outcomes.
qs: In this sense, agentic AI is not simply a cheaper input into existing work; its value depends on whether organizations can redesign workflows, responsibilities, and review processes around delega- tion and verification.
Using job-posting data, they find reduced demand and skill requirements in automation-prone jobs but increased demand and skill complexity in jobs involving human–AI collabo- ration.

st.t: Knowledge work: Task gains do not ensure skill growth
st.an: The source accepts that AI capability or isolated task gains do not by themselves determine workplace value. It materially extends the cluster by shifting analysis to delegated, multi-step workflows and identifying organizational complements—system access, workforce skills, workflow redesign, review and verification—as conditions shaping adoption and realized value, while treating these as interpretations of observed group differences rather than causal estimates.
qs: Large differ-                                                      5 ^Lences across user groups instead suggest that adoption depends on context: access to relevant files and systems, management expectations, workforce skills, and the availability of complementary review pro- cesses.

In this sense, agentic AI is not simply a cheaper input into existing work; its value depends on whether organizations can redesign workflows, responsibilities, and review processes around delega- tion and verification.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Provides concrete usage evidence that agentic AI is reorganizing work around delegated, repeatable workflows while shifting humans toward judgment, oversight and integration. It strengthens the cluster’s emphasis on workflow redesign, verification and organizational complements, although it does not directly test legal competence or apprenticeship risks and treats staffing effects as prospective.
qs: In this sense, agentic AI is not simply a cheaper input into existing work; its value depends on whether organizations can redesign workflows, responsibilities, and review processes around delega- tion and verification.

Agentic systems make it possible to offload larger, more repeatable, and more modu- lar units of work, potentially reducing the importance of some routine execution tasks while increasing the importance of judgment, oversight, coordination, and review.

st.t: Productivity distribution: Weaker users do not always gain most
st.an: The source accepts that AI productivity depends on workflow and complementary human capabilities rather than model access alone, and materially extends the proposition to agentic AI by specifying organizational redesign, delegation, verification and downstream bottlenecks as conditions for converting task-level gains into final output.
qs: In this sense, agentic AI is not simply a cheaper input into existing work; its value depends on whether organizations can redesign workflows, responsibilities, and review processes around delega- tion and verification.
(2026b) show that large task-level productivity gains may translate only imperfectly into final output because downstream human activities remain important bottlenecks.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account of AI as a driver of task reallocation and operating-model redesign rather than demonstrated wholesale replacement. It materially extends that account with usage evidence of delegation, supervision, parallel agents and reusable workflows, while carefully distinguishing usage intensity and requested task complexity from successful completion or realised productivity. Its nonrepresentative OpenAI setting limits generalisation but does not undermine the proposition.
qs: Intensive users appear to manage portfolios of agentic work, with their own role shifting toward delegation, supervision, and integration.
As AI use shifts from consultation to delegation, organizations may need to rethink how work is allocated, reviewed, and coordinated.

kp.k: Agentic AI shifts work from consultation to delegation
kp.d: The authors distinguish conversational assistance from systems that execute multi-step tasks, use tools and modify artifacts. Codex remains rooted in software production but also supports document drafting, data analysis and communication. They qualify the product distinction: in the week preceding June 11, 2026, 60.3% of Codex turns and 21.9% of ChatGPT turns invoked an external tool, and tool use is an imperfect proxy for agency.
qs: Rather than simply asking for information, users increasingly delegate work: producing artifacts, modifying systems, and executing workflows.
In practice, the distinction is not absolute.

kp.k: Evidence compares three differently situated user populations
kp.d: The study analyzes individual accounts, external organizational accounts and OpenAI workers using automated classifiers and aggregated, anonymized usage insights, without researchers reading underlying messages. OpenAI is presented as an unusually favorable adoption environment rather than representative of typical organizations: marginal usage is cheap, organizational support and familiarity are high, and training and knowledge sharing are common. The authors disclose that David Holtz and Prasanna Tambe contributed as paid OpenAI contractors.
qs: Individual users provide a broad-market view of early adoption, where use is heterogeneous and workflow integration is often limited.
However, it provides a view of what agentic AI use may look like in the future, when adoption frictions are minimal.
David Holtz and Prasanna Tambe contributed to this work in their capacity as paid contractors for OpenAI.

kp.k: Rapid adoption remains uneven and concentrated among intensive users
kp.d: Weekly active Codex users increased more than fivefold between January 1 and June 1, 2026, with faster growth among non-developers. In the reported preceding 28-day period, fewer than 1% of active individual users and 17.3% of organizational users used Codex. As of June 11, Codex represented 16.5% of individual, 63.3% of organizational and 99.8% of OpenAI-worker output tokens across Codex and ChatGPT. The paper distinguishes user adoption from token-weighted intensity.
qs: Codex usage grew rapidly after launch, with the number of weekly active users increasing more than fivefold between January 1 and June 1, 2026.
Among individual users, conversational interfaces continue to dominate: fewer than 1% of active individual users used Codex in the last 28 days.
Among organizational users, the corresponding share is 63.3%, while among individual users it is 16.5%.

kp.k: Legal adoption diverges sharply across organizational settings
kp.d: Among external organizational legal users with job-title coverage, Codex accounts for 1.9% of the average user's output tokens but 17.6% of total legal-user tokens, reflecting concentrated intensive use. Within OpenAI, legal and recruiting usage was close to zero in January 2026, reached about 20% by early April, then increased from roughly 20% to 75% within a month. This internal transition coincided with training and regular feedback loops; the authors do not present that coincidence as a causal estimate.
qs: Codex accounts for 17.6% of total output tokens, despite accounting for only 1.9% of tokens generated by the average user.
In January 2026, when engineering users had already shifted more than half of their AI usage to Codex, use in functions such as legal and recruiting was close to zero.
This period coincided with a broader internal effort to adopt Codex across workflows, including training sessions and regular feedback loops.

kp.k: Legal-role token output increases thirteenfold within OpenAI
kp.d: The abstract reports that in June 2026 the median OpenAI employee in a legal role generated 13 times more monthly output tokens across Codex and ChatGPT than in November 2025; the median researcher generated more than 50 times as many. Figure 12 measures trailing-28-day tokens among active users, normalized to November 1, 2025. The authors attribute token growth to both interface switching and more intensive, persistent usage; the reported measure is token output, not a measured increase in completed legal matters or quality.
qs: 13 times more monthly output tokens
while the median researcher generated more than 50 times as many.
This growth in token output reflects several factors, including the shift from conversational interfaces to agentic tools and the later emergence of more intensive, persistent uses of those tools.

kp.k: Software remains dominant as delegated task portfolios broaden
kp.d: The authors find software-related activity across all populations, extending beyond code generation to understanding systems, validation, configuration, repositories and documentation. OpenAI workers exhibit broader research, communication and business-function usage than external organizations. The task taxonomy includes legal and compliance workflows, but its examples are classification definitions rather than separate findings about the frequency or success of particular legal tasks. Figure 5 averages users' classified-request shares; external calculations use a 4% user sample and exclude 'other' messages.
qs: Across all account types, the most common task categories are tied to software production.
This indicates that Codex use, while concentrated in software production, is not limited to producing new code.
Organizational users are more concentrated in coding activities, while OpenAI users show more activity in research, business function workflows, and engineering operations.

kp.d: Using a 0.1% random sample of individual accounts permitting training use, the authors estimate experienced-human completion time from requests. The share of active sampled users submitting at least one request estimated to require an hour rose from 35.4% in December 2025 to 70.2% in May 2026; the eight-hour measure rose from 2.1% to 25.6%. These are estimated requested workloads, not observed human time savings or verified task completions. February and March data are partial, and initial thread turns tend to contain broader tasks than later refinements.
qs: We use the classifier to assign estimated task durations to the prompts sent by a 0.1% random sample of Individual accounts who have opted to allow their data to be used for model training.
This share has increased rapidly—in May 2026, we estimate that 70.2% of users sent at least one prompt of similar or greater difficulty.
The data for February and March is partial.

kp.k: Complexity validation supports ranking rather than precise time equivalence
kp.d: The gpt-5-mini complexity classifier was benchmarked on 1,000 random Codeforces problems. Estimated human completion times correlated 0.65 with the mean completion time of the five fastest solvers and 0.69 with problem difficulty. Predictions generally exceeded observed fastest-solver times, which the authors partly attribute to selection of competitive programmers. They interpret the exercise as evidence that the classifier distinguishes simpler from more complicated tasks.
qs: we apply the classifier to 1,000 random Codeforces problems.
We find that, in general, the model tends to predict slower completion times than the scores derived from the metadata.

kp.k: Parallel agents change delegation and supervision practices
kp.d: For the week prior to June 11, 2026, concurrency means turns in different threads overlapping for more than 30 seconds. Some 67.4% of organizational and 63.9% of individual users had no concurrent turns; most external users who parallelized peaked at two. Only 10.7% of OpenAI users remained at a sole workflow, while nearly 28.6% managed five or more concurrent agents. The authors interpret the internal pattern as humans delegating, managing and reviewing multiple streams of agent work.
qs: Roughly 67.4% of Organizational users and 63.9% of Individual users do not use concurrent turns at all during this period, and among those who do, the majority peak at two concurrent turns.
Only 10.7% of users in this group use a sole workflow at any one time during this period, and nearly 28.6% managed five or more concurrent agents at some point during this period.

kp.k: Long-running execution remains concentrated among frontier users
kp.d: On June 11, 2026, the median OpenAI employee had 2.5 hours of Codex turns running. OpenAI users at the 99th percentile recently accumulated about 71 agent-hours per average day, with cumulative daily runtime increasing nearly 88% since April 7. External 99th-percentile runtime increased roughly 25% for organizational and 50% for individual users during the sample period. Overlapping turns are summed, gaps exceeding 30 minutes are removed, and noninteractive batch-script turns are excluded; runtime is not equivalent to elapsed human labor saved.
qs: on June 11, 2026, the median employee had Codex turns running for 2.5 hours.
Because overlapping turns are summed, a user’s cumulative runtime during a day can exceed 24 hours.
Outside OpenAI, cumulative daily runtime remains substantially lower, and the median user continues to use Codex only intermittently over the course of the day.

kp.k: Reusable skills codify organizational procedures and workflows
kp.d: Skill use among weekly active Codex users rose from 5.4% on March 1 to 26.6% on June 11, 2026. In the seven-day window ending June 11, adoption was 25.7% among individual users, 30.4% among organizational users and 96.2% within OpenAI. The authors distinguish plugins distributing reusable capabilities from custom skills encoding local standards and procedures, arguing that persistent context is especially valuable for repeated, high-context organizational work.
qs: Within OpenAI, skill use is nearly universal: 96.2% of active Codex users invoked at least one skill.
the share of active Codex users invoking any skill rose from 5.4% on March 1, 2026 to 26.6% on June 11, 2026.
Custom skills are especially valuable when repeated tasks depend on organization-specific context, shared conventions, internal procedures, or team-level standards.

kp.k: Seniority differences resist simple junior-versus-manager task divisions
kp.d: Codex's token share rises across seniority levels. External organizations show engineering operations dominating most seniority groups, implementation especially prominent among early-career workers and contractors, and knowledge artifacts more prominent among executives and managers. Within OpenAI, managers and executives devote larger shares to collaboration. The authors reject a simple division between junior implementation and senior management uses; these are cross-domain job classifications, not evidence about law-firm promotion systems.
qs: Codex’s share of output tokens rises across the seniority distribution, indicating that agentic tooling is used by both more junior and more senior workers.

In organizations, engineering operations accounts for the largest share of output tokens for most seniority groups, while code implementation is especially prominent among early-career workers and contractors.

kp.k: Organizational complements condition the value of agentic systems
kp.d: The authors interpret differences across populations as suggesting that capability alone does not determine adoption: access, skills, management expectations and review processes matter. They connect these observations to prior literature, rather than presenting direct causal estimates. They report Hitzig et al.'s argument that delegation raises the importance of supervision, verification, coordination and domain expertise, and Demirer et al.'s finding that downstream human bottlenecks can limit conversion of task-level gains into final output.
qs: If agentic AI adoption depended only on model capability, we would expect similar patterns of use wherever the same model is available.

A central insight from this literature is that productivity gains from new technologies depend on complementary investments in business processes, worker skills, organizational design, and intangible capital.

kp.k: Historical analogy emphasizes redesign rather than simple substitution
kp.d: Drawing on David's account of electrification, the authors argue that major gains followed factory redesign rather than replacing steam engines while preserving layouts. They suggest agentic AI's longer-run potential may similarly depend on reorganizing production, but digital workflow experimentation may be cheaper and diffuse faster than physical plant changes. Concurrency, runtime and skill reuse provide only early, incomplete evidence of organizational redesign.
qs: These changes took decades to diffuse, partly because firms had to incur substantial fixed costs to redesign plants and develop complementary organizational practices.

Whereas electrification often required firms to redesign physical plants and replace durable capital, agentic AI allows workers and organizations to experiment with new workflows at relatively low cost.

kp.k: Workforce restructuring is a prospective implication, not measured displacement
kp.d: The authors suggest that delegating larger, repeatable and modular units of work could reduce the importance of routine execution while increasing judgment, oversight, coordination and review. They predict possible changes to team composition, hiring, career ladders and skill-level allocation, rather than reporting measured legal-job losses or law-firm restructuring. They also recommend supplementing conventional adoption measures with indicators of delegated work and workflow organization.
qs: These changes could affect team composition, hiring needs, career ladders, and the distribution of work across skill levels.
Future analyses may need to track delegated task complexity, runtime, workflow reuse, concurrency, and production output.
The frontier of AI adoption is therefore moving from asking systems for answers toward managing systems that act.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Johnston and co-authors describe a shift from conversational assistance toward delegated production, with rapid but uneven adoption and potential changes to knowledge-work roles.
pts.d: This is primarily a cross-domain study of Codex use, rather than a study of legal-service markets. The authors report that weekly active Codex users increased more than fivefold between January 1 and June 1, 2026, with faster growth among non-developers. Codex's share of output tokens across Codex and ChatGPT reached 99.8% for OpenAI workers, 63.3% for external organizational users, and 16.5% for individual users as of June 11. Legal-specific findings illustrate the uneven transition: among external organizational legal users, Codex represented 1.9% of the average user's output tokens but 17.6% of aggregate output tokens. Within OpenAI, legal and recruiting functions shifted from near-zero Codex shares in January to about 20% in early April and roughly 75% within another month. The abstract reports that the median OpenAI employee in a legal role generated 13 times as many monthly output tokens across the two products in June 2026 as in November 2025. These are usage and token-output findings, not measured increases in completed legal work or legal-service productivity. More broadly, the authors interpret concurrent agents, longer runtimes, and reusable workflows as signs that intensive users increasingly delegate, supervise, review, and integrate work. They predict possible changes to routine execution, team composition, hiring, career ladders, and allocation of work across skill levels, without estimating job losses or legal-market effects.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The findings rest on observational product-usage data and automated classification; organizational and employment implications are interpretations and predictions rather than measured causal outcomes.
pts.d: The authors compare personal accounts, Business and Enterprise accounts, and OpenAI workers using aggregated, anonymized usage data. They measure active users, output tokens, task mix, estimated task complexity, concurrent turns, runtime, and reusable skill invocation. External role comparisons use firms with high-quality job-title information; internal adoption-by-function comparisons use OpenAI job-function metadata. Different analyses use different samples: persona growth uses a 3% user sample, task-composition analyses use 4% samples, and complexity estimates use a 0.1% random sample of individual accounts whose users allowed training use. The model estimates the hands-on time an experienced human would require, rather than measuring actual hours saved or successful completion. Between December 2025 and May 2026, the share submitting at least one request estimated to require eight human hours rose from 2.1% to 25.6%. Validation on 1,000 Codeforces problems produced correlations of 0.65 with mean solve times for the five fastest humans and 0.69 with problem difficulty; this is coding-based benchmarking, not validation of legal-task performance. Concurrency, runtime, and skill-use measures support the workflow interpretation: 28.6% of OpenAI users peaked at five or more concurrent agents in the observed week, and skill use reached 96.2% internally, versus 30.4% for organizational and 25.7% for individual users. The paper also draws on prior research and the historical analogy of electrification to motivate predictions about organizational complements. Those cited studies are not original findings of this paper. The research is produced by OpenAI-affiliated authors, including two disclosed paid contractors.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The empirical claims concern adoption through June 11, 2026; wider workforce restructuring is conditional and has no specified completion date.
pts.d: The main adoption-growth claim concerns January through June 2026, while several comparisons extend back into 2025. Many reported measures use trailing 28-day windows; concurrency and skill-use comparisons use the week ending June 11, 2026. Figure 12 normalizes trailing-28-day median token output to November 1, 2025; the abstract summarizes the legal-role comparison as June 2026 versus November 2025. The authors explicitly treat OpenAI as an unusually favorable frontier setting, not a representative organization: marginal usage costs are low, quantity restrictions are absent, familiarity and organizational support are high, and training and informal knowledge-sharing are common. The internal adoption acceleration coincided with training and feedback efforts, rather than establishing their causal effect. Broader diffusion depends on relevant system access, permissions, security requirements, workforce skills, management expectations, and review processes. Claims about faster workflow experimentation and longer-run productivity are possibilities, not dated forecasts. Typical use also remains intermittent, despite intensive use at the upper tail. The paper qualifies the conversational-versus-agentic distinction because both products can have agentic and conversational interactions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The source concerns software developers and broader knowledge workers, including legal-function staff; it does not establish effects on law-firm business models or access to justice.
pts.d: Developers lead adoption, but the authors report expansion into research, planning, communication, recruiting, sales, product work, data analysis, and legal functions. OpenAI's legal workers are on the corporate in-house side, not a sample of law-firm providers. External organizational legal-role classifications include counsel and paralegals, but the reported findings do not isolate law firms, ALSPs, or particular legal-market segments. Across occupations, adoption extends through the seniority distribution: early-career workers and contractors show relatively prominent code implementation, while executives and managers devote larger shares to knowledge artifacts or collaboration. The authors caution against a simple junior-implementation versus senior-management division. They suggest that workers may increasingly coordinate multiple agent workstreams and that employers may revise responsibilities, review processes, hiring, and career structures. The source does not quantify client savings, legal accuracy, professional liability, changes in lawyer headcount, or unmet civil legal need. Its legal-and-compliance taxonomy lists contract review, policy checks, controls, audits, approvals, and regulatory documentation, but these labels should not be read as demonstrated success rates or legal-task-specific productivity results.
